title: Manipuri Musician Beaten to Death in Delhi, Reigniting Racial Violence Fears
excerpt: Chongtham Vikram Singh, 54, was fatally assaulted outside his home after confronting a group about noise, sparking protests and renewed demands for Northeast community safety.
body:
• Chongtham Vikram Singh, a 54-year-old Manipuri musician and music teacher, was fatally assaulted in southeast Delhi on September 7 after confronting a group about noise outside his home
  • Eight people, including a 15-year-old minor, have been arrested under mob-lynching and murder provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
  • The killing has triggered candlelight marches and renewed concerns about racial discrimination against people from India's Northeast
  • Manipur's Chief Minister has written to Delhi's CM demanding a high-level investigation into the incident

A Noise Complaint Turned Fatal

Chongtham Vikram Singh, a 54-year-old musician and music teacher from Manipur, was beaten to death outside his home in Kilokari village, southeast Delhi, on the night of September 7 after he confronted a group of men about noise and disturbance near his residence.

https://x.com/IndianExpress/status/2097232802345587041

According to police and family accounts, Singh stepped out of his third-floor apartment around 11:30 p.m. to confront delivery workers and dhaba staff who were reportedly drinking and shouting outside his building. What began as a verbal argument turned violent within minutes. The group allegedly chased Singh back into the building corridor, where they kicked and punched him repeatedly before fleeing.

Singh's son, Yaiphaba, told police he opened his door to find four to five men attacking his father. When he raised an alarm, the assailants fled. Yaiphaba and his mother rushed Singh by taxi to Holy Family Hospital, where he died hours later from hemorrhagic shock caused by blunt-force injuries.

Eight Arrested, Investigation Underway

Delhi Police arrested seven men and apprehended a 15-year-old juvenile within hours of the attack. The arrested men — Bharat Kumar (19), Pramod (26), Ramzan Khan (22), Deepanshu (21), Mohan Vishwakarma (32), Vijay (36), and Mannu (26) — all worked at local food stalls as delivery or packaging workers, according to police.

A case has been registered under sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita dealing with murder by a group and common intent. CCTV footage from Singh's building, shared online by former Manipur Chief Minister N. Biren Singh, shows the group leaving the scene immediately after the assault. Deputy Commissioner of Police Vineet Kumar said senior officers met with Singh's family and assured them of a thorough investigation.

A Pioneer of Manipuri Rock

Singh was no ordinary musician. In Manipur, he was recognized as a rock pioneer and the lead guitarist of Eastern Dark — a band whose name itself was a statement about the political marginalization of India's northeastern communities. He had also played with bands Ultra Vires and Phoenix before moving to Delhi, where he spent two decades teaching music and mentoring young musicians through private classes.

"Why do others not think of us as Indians?"

— A question raised by Northeast community members following Singh's killing

Racial Fears Resurface

By Monday evening, nearly 100 people from Delhi's Northeast community gathered in Kilokari for a candlelight march demanding justice. The killing has reopened deep wounds about racial discrimination and violence faced by people from northeastern India in the country's metropolitan cities.

The North East Media Forum condemned the killing and demanded that "any possibility of racial or identity-based targeting must be thoroughly investigated." The forum said it was deeply concerned by "increasing reports and incidents of targeted violence, intimidation and discrimination against people from the North East, particularly where there may be racial prejudice or discriminatory attitudes."

People from India's northeastern states — whose East Asian features set them apart from the rest of the country's population — have long reported being subjected to racial slurs, social exclusion, and violence in cities like Delhi. Rights groups have documented hundreds of such incidents over the past decade, though few have resulted in hate-crime prosecutions.

Police have said no racial motive has been established so far. But community leaders insist the possibility cannot be dismissed until a comprehensive investigation is completed.

Political Fallout

The killing has drawn sharp political reactions. Manipur Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh wrote to Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta demanding a high-level probe. Congress MP Pawan Khera accused the state and central governments of fostering a "culture of impunity."

"The government may not have wielded the bat that killed Vikram Singh. But it cannot escape responsibility for creating the environment that led to his murder."

— Pawan Khera, Congress MP

Manipur MP Bimol Akoijam demanded exemplary punishment for those responsible, while activist Binalaxmi Nepram stayed with the family through the night as the post-mortem was completed at AIIMS.

What Comes Next

The investigation continues, with police working to establish whether any racial motive was involved. Community organizations have vowed to press for a thorough probe and are planning further demonstrations if progress stalls.

For Delhi's Northeast community, Singh's death is both a personal tragedy and a grimly familiar pattern — one that forces the question of whether India's capital can truly be a safe city for all its residents, regardless of where they come from.
nri_angle: The killing highlights persistent racial discrimination against Northeast Indians, a concern that resonates with diaspora communities who face similar identity-based challenges abroad.
author: Diaspora Desk
